extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarizing the American sitcom Murphy Brown, covering its premise, characters, production history, revival, reception, cultural impact, syndication, and awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topicality / attention to current events
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to current events – which became old – is one of the reasons that 'Murphy Brown' was never as big in syndication as expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes that many episodes contained topical news and cultural references that "had quickly become dated," reducing off-network syndication appeal. Evaluations of long-term success should consider whether a show's topicality will age well for future audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of sensitive subjects (storyline sensitivity and public-health impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's handling of [breast cancer] was credited with a 30 percent increase in the number of women getting mammograms that year, and Bergen was presented an award from the American Cancer Society in honor of her role in educating women on the importance of breast cancer prevention and screening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storylines dealing with medical or controversial issues can generate both controversy (e.g., attacks by conservative groups over medical marijuana scenes) and measurable public-health outcomes; quality assessment should weigh both the sensitivity/accuracy of portrayal and its societal impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and political impact (capacity to spark public debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dan Quayle criticized single parenting during his 1992 speech, which caused a public discussion on family values and led the show to respond in a season premiere that showcased and celebrated the diversity of the modern American family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A program's influence on public discourse and its ability to engage or respond to political controversies are considered markers of cultural impact; assess whether the show shapes debate, elicits reactions from public figures, and integrates real-world commentary into its narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting decisions, continuity, and guest stars
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival production approached original cast members; Candice Bergen agreed to return on the condition that Faith Ford, Joe Regalbuto, and Grant Shaud join as well. The revival included prominent guest appearances (e.g., Hillary Clinton secret cameo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting continuity (bringing back original cast) and the use of high-profile guest stars are presented as important factors for a revival's reception and promotional appeal. Evaluations should consider ensemble chemistry and star power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception criteria (nostalgia, wit, and messaging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotten Tomatoes' critical consensus: "This just in: while the nostalgia and wit are welcome, Murphy Brown's dated messaging tactics feel heavy-handed and smug, leaving this formerly formidably timely series feeling like a reboot reaching for the headlines."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical appraisal often balances positive elements (nostalgia, wit) against negatives (dated or heavy-handed messaging). Use aggregated critic scores (Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic) and consensus language to understand how reviewers weigh these dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewership, ratings and network renewal/cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: Season-by-season tables list rank, average rating, and average viewers; the revival was canceled by CBS after one season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is measured by Nielsen-style ratings, rank, and average viewers; these figures materially influence network decisions on renewals, episode orders, scheduling, and cancellations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndication and home-media viability (music licensing and sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Murphy Brown was unsuccessful when introduced in off-network syndication in the 1990s in part because of costly music rights fees; Warner Home Video released only the first season on DVD due to low sales and high music licensing costs, and no future releases are planned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical factors such as music-licensing costs and home-media sales can limit syndication and DVD releases regardless of a show's critical reputation; consider licensing encumbrances when evaluating long-term distribution potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and industry recognition as quality signals
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents Emmys, Golden Globes, Peabody Awards, and rankings (e.g., Murphy ranked #25 on TV Guide Network's 25 Greatest TV Characters of All Time) associated with the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry awards and inclusion on 'best of' lists serve as formal indicators of peer and industry recognition; they are useful metrics when assessing a show's historical standing and perceived quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network production decisions and episode orders affecting revival outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: CBS gave the revival a series order for one season of thirteen episodes, extended the premiere running time by five minutes, and later canceled the revival after one season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions such as episode order size, premiere runtime, scheduling, and promotional strategy by the network influence a show's ability to find an audience and succeed; these business/operational factors should be included in evaluations of production outcomes.
